A plate occupies the region $D$ enclosed by the lines $y=0$, $x=4$, and the curve $y=\sqrt{x}$, as shown above. If the mass density function of $D$ is given by $\lambda (x,y)=3y,$ find the moment of inertia of the lamina about the origin.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 4,\,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{x}},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14069995/assets/dd5ee021dd73317a775c0ea653212f7ee5545f8c6854e6a9daabdc93b5c3b9c0.png)

Using the formula for ${I}_{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot 3y\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{x}}3{x}^{2}y+3{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{[\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{3}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}\frac{3}{2}{x}^{3}+\frac{3}{4}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{3}{8}{x}^{4}+\frac{1}{4}{x}^{3}]}_{0}^{4} \\  & =96+16 \\  & =112.\end{aligned}
$$

A rectangular plate occupies the region
$D={(x,y)\,:\,0\le x\le 3,\,\,0\le y\le 1}$
with mass density function $\lambda (x,y)=(4y+1)\,\text{kg}/{\text{m}}^{2},$ where $x$ and $y$ area measured in meters. Find the moment of inertia of this lamina about the origin.
questions.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda (x,y),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{x}={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is given by

$$
{I}_{y}={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
{I}_{0}={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A={I}_{x}+{I}_{y}.
$$

Using the formula for ${I}_{0},$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{0} & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\lambda (x,y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})(4y+1)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{3}4{x}^{2}y+{x}^{2}+4{y}^{3}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{4}{3}{x}^{3}y+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}+4x{y}^{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{x=0}^{x=3}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}36y+9+12{y}^{3}+3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =[18{y}^{2}+9y+3{y}^{4}+{y}^{3}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =18+9+3+1 \\  & =31.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia of the lamina about the origin is $31\,\text{kg}\cdot {\text{m}}^{2}.$

$$

$$

$$

$$
I_y =  \iint\limits_D x^2\lambda(x,y)  \:\textrm{d}A.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin is given by

$$
I_0 = \iint\limits_D (x^2+y^2) \lambda(x,y)  \:\textrm{d}A = I_x + I_y.
$$

First, notice that $D$ is a type I region with representation

$$
D = \left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \:\: x^2 \leq y \leq 1 \right\},
$$

as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14069995/assets/8846da0fe3b1e8369a9277bbaba1e082d040136a71105a5816af7b13d2788027.png)

$$

$$

canonical_examples.worked_solution:
For a plane lamina $D$ with mass density function $\lambda(r,\theta),$ we have the following definitions:

- The moment of inertia about the $x$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
I_x = \iint\limits_D \lambda(r,\theta) \cdot r^3\sin^2{\theta} \:\textrm{d}r\:\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the $y$-axis, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
I_y = \iint\limits_D \lambda(r,\theta) \cdot  r^3\cos^2{\theta} \:\textrm{d}r\:\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

- The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is given by

$$
I_0 = \iint\limits_D \lambda(r,\theta) \cdot  r^3 \:\textrm{d}r\:\textrm{d}\theta = I_x + I_y.
$$

First, note that the region $D$ in polar coordinates can be expressed as

$$
D = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 1 \leq r \leq 2, \:\: \dfrac{\pi}{6} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{4} \right\}.
$$

Also, the mass density function in polar coordinates is 

$$
\lambda(r,\theta) = \dfrac{1}{r^2 \cos^2{\theta}}.
$$

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the $y$-axis is

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{y} & ={∬}_{D}\lambda (r,\theta )\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{1}^{2}\frac{1}{{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\cdot {r}^{3}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /4}{\int }_{1}^{2}r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =({\int }_{1}^{2}r\,\text{d}r)({\int }_{\pi /6}^{\pi /4}\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{r}^{2}\,{|}_{1}^{2}\cdot \theta \,{|}_{\pi /6}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(4-1)\cdot (\frac{\pi }{4}-\frac{\pi }{6}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 3\cdot \frac{\pi }{12} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{8}.\end{aligned}
$$
